sentences.text: Caipirasuchus represents a vanished lineage of sphagesaurid notosuchians, a group of crocodile-like reptiles.
The primary specimens include an almost complete skull and lower jaw with only a few missing teeth, alongside partial body parts.
Scientists have identified roughly ten unique physical traits that distinguish this genus from all others.
In the upper jaw, the nostril opening is framed entirely by premaxilla bones, each holding four teeth.
Gaps separate the front teeth from the rest of the upper row, while the lower jaw features ten teeth per side divided by two spaces.
The front teeth were shaped for seizing prey, whereas the rear teeth processed food.
One species possesses a special internal chamber connected to airways that likely aided in making sounds.
A species was named in 2021 to honor the famous naturalist David Attenborough.
The genus was first defined by Iori and Carvalho in 2011, establishing the type species C. paulistanus that same year.
The holotype was unearthed on the São Francisco Farm in Monte Alto County, within the Adamantina Formation of the Bauru Basin.
Additional species were added later, including one moved from Sphagesaurus in 2013, another described in 2014, and a third in 2018.
The name blends the Tupi word for traditional São Paulo residents with the Greek term for crocodile.
More species were identified in 2021 from the Santo Anastácio Formation and in 2024 from the Adamantina Formation.
This animal belongs to the subfamily Caipirasuchinae and is classified within the family Sphagesauridae.
Fossils date to the Late Cretaceous, spanning from 93.9 million years ago down to the end of the Maastrichtian stage.
Remains have been recovered from northern São Paulo State and western Minas Gerais State in southeastern Brazil.
